analysis.one_liner: Requires the biggest banks to hold far more equity capital and bans federal bailouts of their non-bank arms.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill that would have forced the largest banks to hold at least 8% equity capital — 15% for the very biggest — and barred future bailouts died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The TBTF Act would have required every large bank to hold a set share of its own money — equity capital — against its assets, starting at 8% for banks over $50 billion and rising to at least 15% for the giants over $500 billion. It would have cut off federal rescue money — Fed emergency lending, Deposit Insurance Fund draws, Treasury programs — to bank affiliates that aren't insured deposits, ending the expectation that taxpayers or the safety net will backstop Wall Street bets. It also bundled regulatory relief for community banks, including an easier definition of 'rural' for mortgage rules, an examination ombudsman, and exemptions from some disclosure and data-collection rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would face a lower risk of footing the bill when a giant bank fails; bank depositors and anyone exposed to a financial crash, since banks with more of their own capital fail less often; and community banks, which get targeted relief from reporting and examination burdens.

how_it_helps.text: Requires banks with more than $50 billion in assets to hold at least 8% equity capital against total assets, and banks with at least $500 billion to hold at least 15%, with a surcharge that rises as size increases [S2][S3].

Prohibits federal assistance — asset purchases, government loans, capital injections, Fed lending under sections 13 and 13A, the Exchange Stabilization Fund, and the Deposit Insurance Fund — to non-bank affiliates of financial institutions, except during resolution of a failed institution [S2][S3].
Requires capital rules to apply to every affiliate and subsidiary of a big bank holding company, closing the gap that let risk sit in unregulated corners of a banking group [S2][S3].
Includes anti-evasion provisions allowing regulators to force divestiture of structures designed to slip under the asset thresholds [S3].

Provides relief for community banks: a broader rural definition for qualified mortgage rules, an independent examination ombudsman, exemption from annual written privacy notices when policies haven't changed, and an exemption from small-business lending data collection for banks under $10 billion [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest banks and their shareholders, who would have to raise hundreds of billions in equity capital, shrinking returns and the volume of lending those banks can support; some borrowers could face tighter credit from the biggest institutions.
analysis.who_pays_short: The largest banks and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill prohibits any further implementation of the Basel III capital accord, replacing negotiated international risk-based standards with a simpler leverage measure — a trade its supporters accepted to secure bipartisan backing, but one that critics said could allow more concentration in risky assets in some cases [S3].

Requiring the biggest banks to hold up to 15% equity capital would raise their funding costs; an honest supporter would acknowledge that some of that cost can be passed to borrowers as tighter credit or higher rates from the largest institutions.

The community-bank relief package includes exemptions from small-business lending data collection under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and from annual written privacy notices, reducing public visibility into which small businesses get credit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: much higher capital would make the biggest banks far harder to topple and dramatically cut the odds of another taxpayer-funded rescue, at the price of somewhat costlier credit from those institutions. The Basel III prohibition and some of the data-collection exemptions are genuine concessions that weaken parts of the framework, but the bill's central mechanism — a hard, rising equity floor with an end to non-bank bailout channels — is the strongest version of this reform that reached the Senate in that Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It never got a vote: the Senate Banking Committee took no action after referring the bill, and the full Congress ended without a markup or floor vote.

narrative.text: Introduced April 24, 2013 by Sen. Sherrod Brown with Sens. Vitter, Kirk, and Sessions, and read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S5][S3].
It gathered 7 cosponsors split 3 Republicans, 3 Democrats, and 1 Independent [S4].
The only further action was a January 8, 2014 hearing on financial institutions in a Banking Committee subcommittee; no markup was ever scheduled and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 113th Congress without a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest banks came out ahead: they avoided a hard 8% equity floor, a 15% requirement for the giants, and a statutory ban on the federal rescue channels they relied on in 2008. Community banks also kept the existing regulatory structure the bill would have eased.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest banks, which avoided higher capital

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed for higher capital requirements and an end to bailouts for the largest banks.

for.name: Sens. David Vitter, Mark Kirk, and Jeff Sessions
for.role: U.S. Senators (R-LA, R-IL, R-AL), original Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined Brown in introducing the bill, making its launch bipartisan.

for.name: 7 cosponsors (3 Republicans, 3 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on to the bill, giving it support from both parties.

for.name: Large-bank opponents of the Brown-Vitter proposal
for.role: Largest U.S. banks and their trade groups
for.what_they_did: Lobbied against sharply higher capital requirements, arguing the 8% and 15% floors would constrain lending and put U.S. banks at a competitive disadvantage.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over bank regulation in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and held only a subcommittee hearing on financial institutions; never scheduled a markup or a vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — original cosponsorship came from one Democrat and three Republicans, and the full cosponsor list split 3 Republicans, 3 Democrats, and 1 Independent — but the committee never brought it to a vote.

industries.industry: The largest banks (over $50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to hold at least 8% equity capital — 15% for those over $500 billion — and cut off federal rescue channels for their non-bank arms, directly reducing their profits and the implicit government backstop behind their funding. Their loss would have been the public's gain in bailout and crash risk, which is why their interest ran against the bill.

industries.industry: Community banks and small savings associations (under $50 billion)
industries.note: They would have kept capital rules comparable to those in effect May 2013 and received targeted relief: a broader rural definition for mortgage rules, an examination ombudsman, exemption from annual written privacy notices, and an exemption from small-business lending data collection under $10 billion in assets. Their gain was modest relief without imposing costs on the public.

industries.industry: Insurance and securities affiliates of banking groups
industries.note: The bill would have extended the bank-level equity rules down to every affiliate and subsidiary, and barred them from federal assistance — ending the subsidy of cheap, safety-net-backed funding flowing into non-bank businesses inside banking conglomerates.
